syllabus.clause: clustering matched record pairs into entities

at.step: A customer table holds the same person many times, spelled differently, and a matcher scores every candidate pair. One pair with a middling score joins two large clusters into a single person. Predict: raise the threshold slightly past that pair's score — does the biggest cluster split into a few pieces or many, and does the cluster count change smoothly as the threshold rises?

Union-find, the textbook structure underneath this topic: find follows parent pointers up to a root, the entity id, compressing the path as it goes; union joins two roots by size. Nothing here is new; Chapter 11 built and proved this structure already.

The chapter's own match graph: twenty-four records in three groups of eight. Inside each group, strong-scoring pairs hold it together. Between groups, exactly two deliberately weak pairs are the only bridges — the entire setup for everything that follows.

Splink's own documentation, read at research time: cluster_pairwise_predictions_at_threshold clusters the pairwise match predictions into groups of connected records using the connected components graph clustering algorithm. One union per matching pair; one find per entity id. Nothing more is needed.

Trace one record's entity id as every scored pair lands, strongest first: it stays its own root through nearly the whole stream, because its own group is strong enough to need no outside help. Only the last two pairs, the weak bridges, finally pull it into the whole graph's single component.

syllabus.clause: and connected components in lineage graphs

at.step: The same structure, a different graph: vertices are datasets and jobs, edges are feeds-into dependencies. A connected component here is a blast radius — everything that could be touched by a change to any one member. The chapter's own small lineage graph splits into one component of six and one of three.

On one machine, union-find needs one shared parent array. GraphFrames' own connectedComponents, read from source, is not that: an iterative algorithm, its own default now called two_phase, with a checkpoint interval, because no single machine holds the whole structure to update in place. Predict: on the chapter's own small match graph, does a round-based alternative with no shared structure take fewer rounds than union-find's one pass, the same number, or many more?

Ten rounds against one pass, on the identical twenty-four-record graph, converging to the identical clustering either way. The cost is not correctness; both methods land on the same two clusters. The cost is communication: ten rounds of every node talking to its neighbors, against one machine walking an edge list once.

The sweep, measured: at or below the lower bridge's score, one cluster of twenty-four. Cross it, and the graph splits into sixteen and eight. Cross the second bridge, and it splits again into eight, eight and eight. Two jumps across six tested thresholds, exactly where the predict question asked about.

Lower the threshold back below where it was, and the two groups merge again — but there is no operation that un-merges them at the higher threshold once they have joined. Union-find has no split operation: once two roots are joined, the only way back is rebuilding the whole clustering from the edge list at the new threshold.
